summary: Routing information reduction through BGP route reflection or confederation can lead to persistent internal route oscillations in certain topologies. This proposed standard specifies two sets of additional paths that can be advertised to eliminate those oscillations.

eli5.summary: Sometimes routers keep changing their minds back and forth forever. This shows how to share a few more route choices so they settle down and stop flip-flopping.

questions: what causes bgp persistent route oscillation
what are bgp group best paths
how does add-path fix med oscillation
what is med induced route oscillation
subtitle: Two sets of extra BGP paths that route reflectors and confederation border routers can advertise to stop persistent route oscillation.

tldr.problem: Route reflection and confederations reduce routing information inside a network, and with certain setups and topologies this can cause persistent internal BGP route oscillation, usually involving the MED attribute.
tldr.mechanism: A route reflector or confederation border router advertises more than its single best path, using ADD-PATH: either all available paths, or only the best path from each neighboring AS (the Group Best Paths).
tldr.outcome: Advertising all paths gives the same consistency as a full IBGP mesh, and Group Best Paths are enough to remove MED-induced oscillation if common design practice and topological constraints hold.

today: RFC 7964 is a Proposed Standard and the data shows no obsoleting or updating RFC, so it stands as the specification of these two path sets. It builds on the ADD-PATH mechanism in RFC 7911.

sections.title: The Oscillation Problem
sections.content:
As documented in RFC 3345, routing information reduction by BGP Route Reflection (RFC 4456) or BGP Confederation (RFC 5065) can cause persistent Internal BGP (IBGP) route oscillations in certain routing setups and topologies. Except for a couple of artificially engineered topologies, the MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) attribute from RFC 4271 has played a pivotal role in virtually all known cases. The RFC calls these "MED-induced route oscillations".

To eliminate them, a route reflector or confederation ASBR needs to advertise more than just the best path for an address prefix. The RFC describes two sets of paths that can be advertised, and says they can be sent using the ADD-PATH mechanism (RFC 7911). It assumes nothing beyond the base BGP specification.
sections.eli5: Sometimes routers keep changing their favorite route again and again and never settle. The fix is for the helper routers to share a few more choices instead of just one.

sections.title: Advertising All Available Paths
sections.content:
In a network with a full IBGP mesh, all BGP speakers have consistent and equivalent routing information, so such a network is free of MED-induced oscillation and of other inconsistencies such as forwarding loops. The first approach copies that: let a route reflector or confederation ASBR advertise all the available paths for a prefix. This gives the same amount of routing information and consistency as the full mesh.

For scalability, the RFC says the advertisement of multiple paths should be limited to prefixes affected by MED-induced oscillation in a network with many alternate paths. How a node detects such a condition locally is outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: The simplest fix is to tell everyone about every route you know. Then everyone has the same picture and has nothing to argue about.

sections.title: Advertising the Group Best Paths
sections.content:
The neighbor-AS of a route is the neighboring autonomous system from which it was received. MED is comparable only among routes with the same neighbor-AS. So route selection can be seen as two steps: group the paths for a prefix by neighbor-AS and pick the most preferred in each group (the Group Best Path), then pick the overall best among those.

The second approach advertises all the Group Best Paths. It relies on a widely adopted practice recommended in RFC 4456 and RFC 5065: design a cluster or sub-AS so that routes from inside it are preferred over routes from other clusters when the decision is by IGP cost to the BGP NEXT_HOP, typically by setting IGP metrics inside a cluster much smaller than between clusters. When that holds, the RFC claims Group Best Paths are sufficient to eliminate MED-induced oscillation, and Appendix A argues why.

A Group Best Path is identified by the prefix plus the neighbor-AS, so with ADD-PATH the neighbor-AS may serve as the path identifier. This approach still needs certain topological constraints, described in RFC 3345.
sections.eli5: Instead of sharing every route, each router shares just the best one from each neighboring network. That is far fewer, and still enough to stop the flip-flopping.

sections.title: Changes to Route Reflection and Confederation
sections.content:
Both approaches use the ADD-PATH Capability. For a given AFI/SAFI, the speaker MUST include it in the capability it advertises with the Send/Receive field set to 2 (send multiple paths) or 3 (send/receive). The procedures below apply when the peer also advertises 1 (receive multiple paths) or 3 for the same AFI/SAFI.

Route reflector. To a client peer it MUST advertise the Group Best Paths (or Available Paths) received from its non-client IBGP peers, and MAY also advertise those received from its clients. To a non-client peer it MUST advertise those received from its clients.

Confederation ASBR. To an internal peer it MUST advertise the paths received from its confederation-external peers. To a confederation-external peer it MUST advertise the paths received from its IBGP peers.
sections.eli5: Each helper router follows rules about who should hear which extra routes, so every group gets the extra choices it needs.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Some oscillations, once detected, can be removed by simple configuration workarounds. Carrying extra paths costs memory and convergence time, so the RFC recommends weighing that impact and considering a workaround before deploying, and again limiting multiple paths to affected prefixes.

Route reflectors and confederation ASBRs must advertise the extra paths, but the vast majority of BGP speakers only need to receive them, which involves only minor software changes.

Group Best Paths are expected to be adequate for the vast majority of networks. The number of paths a reflector advertises is bounded by the number of neighbor-ASes for a prefix, and that number is typically small. However, they may be inadequate to avoid other inconsistencies such as forwarding loops, and the required topological constraints could be operationally challenging. In those cases Available Paths may be used, limited to affected prefixes.
sections.eli5: Sharing more routes uses more memory, so only do it where there is a real problem. Most networks will be fine with the smaller, cheaper option.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states a single point: this extension to BGP does not change the underlying security issues inherent in the existing BGP specification, RFC 4271. It adds no new security mechanism and names no new threat.
sections.eli5: Sharing extra routes does not make BGP any safer or any riskier than it already was.
